concepts.title: The Failure of Point Prediction: Multimodal Distributions
concepts.one_liner: A point estimate can fail badly when the true data distribution is multimodal, as it can only represent one mode and may predict an invalid average.
concepts.content:
We could formulate the problem as least-squares regression: train a function to output a vector of real-valued numbers representing the red, green, and blue values of every pixel in the image, then penalize the squared distance between these values and the ground truth values. This kind of regression fits a function $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$. For every input $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}$, the output is a single point prediction $\hat{\mathbf{y}} \in \mathcal{Y}$, meaning just one prediction of what the value of $\mathbf{y}$ should be.

(see figure: Different kinds of predictive distributions.)

What if there are multiple equally valid answers? Taking a color image and making it grayscale is a many-to-one mapping: for any given grayscale value, there are many different color values that could have projected to that gray. This means the colorization problem is fundamentally ambiguous, and there may be multiple valid color solutions for any grayscale input. A point estimate is bound to be a poor inference since it can only predict one solution.

Figure @fig-conditional_generative_models-tshirts shows several kinds of predictions given a grayscale t-shirt. The question is: What is the color of the shirt? To unify different prediction models, we represent them all as outputting a distribution over possible shirt colors. Let $A$ be a random variable representing the $a$ value of the shirt in $lab$ color space. Our input is the $l$ value of the shirt. Our predictions are represented as $p_{\theta}(A \mid l)$. The particular shirt comes in two colors, teal or pink. The true data distribution $p_{\texttt{data}}$ is two delta functions, one on teal and one on pink.

Least-squares regression results in a model that predicts the mean of the data distribution. Therefore, the point prediction output by a least-squares regressor will be that the shirt is gray. The probability density associated with this prediction is shown in @fig-conditional_generative_models-tshirts (b).

A point prediction does not necessarily come with probabilistic semantics, but here we interpret a prediction $\hat{a} = f_{\theta}(l)$ as implying a predictive distribution $p_{\theta}(A = a \mid l) = \delta(a - \hat{a})$, where $\delta$ is the Dirac delta function.

This prediction is entirely wrong! It splits the difference between the two true possibilities and results in zero probability under the data distribution. Using a different loss function (e.g., $L_1$ loss instead of $L_2$) would yield a different solution, but never the correct one. Because the true distribution has two equally probable modes, a single point prediction can only represent one mode.

We can do better by predicting a distribution rather than a point.
concepts.motivation_md: Point predictions fail for multimodal distributions because they average multiple valid outcomes into an invalid single prediction, motivating probabilistic or distributional prediction methods.
concepts.recap_md:
- Least-squares regression outputs a single point prediction $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$.
- Multimodal true distributions cannot be captured by a single point estimate.
- Point predictions average modes, resulting in invalid predictions with zero true probability.

example.text: The question is straightforward: What is the color of the shirt? To unify different kinds of prediction models, we will represent them all as outputting a distribution over the possible colors of the shirt. Let $A$ be a random variable that represents the $a$ value of the shirt in $lab$ color space. Our input is just the $l$ value of the shirt. The true data distribution, $p_{\texttt{data}}$, is therefore two delta functions, one on teal and the other on pink.

concepts.title: structured prediction

position.section_title: Conditional Generative Models Solve Multimodal Structured Prediction

concepts.one_liner: Structured prediction methods model joint structure in the output space without factorizing outputs into independent potentials.
concepts.content: Methods that model joint structure in the output space are called structured prediction methods—they don't factorize the output into independent potentials conditioned on the input. Conditional generative modeling is a structured prediction approach that models a full distribution of possibilities over the joint configuration of outputs.
concepts.motivation_md: Structured prediction methods exist to capture dependencies among output variables, enabling more accurate modeling of complex outputs than independent predictions. (LLM-inferred)
concepts.recap_md:
- Structured prediction models joint output structure without factorization.
- Conditional generative modeling is a structured prediction approach.
- These methods model full distributions over joint output configurations.

concepts.title: amortized inference

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: Amortized inference learns a direct mapping from inputs to outputs to approximate exact inference, amortizing inference cost over training.
concepts.content: Amortized inference is where the cost of inference is amortized over a training phase. This training phase learns a direct mapping from inputs to outputs that approximates the solution we would have gotten if we did exact inference on that input.
concepts.motivation_md: Amortized inference reduces the computational cost of inference by learning a direct approximation, enabling efficient predictions at test time. (LLM-inferred)
concepts.recap_md:
- Amortized inference spreads inference cost over training.
- It learns a direct input-to-output mapping.
- This approximates exact inference efficiently at test time.

concepts.title: Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: Conditional GANs add input $\mathbf{x}$ to both generator and discriminator, making the discriminator judge input-output pairs as real or synthetic.
concepts.content:
We can make a generative adversarial network (GAN) conditional by adding $\mathbf{x}$ as an input to both the generator and the discriminator:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \arg\min_{\theta}\max_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z},\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})) \big]
\end{aligned}$$

This changes the discriminator's job from asking "is the output real or synthetic?" to asking "is the input-output *pair* real or synthetic?" An input-output pair can be considered synthetic for two reasons:

1. The output looks synthetic.
2. The output does not match the input.

If both reasons are avoided, it can be shown that the produced samples are iid with respect to the true conditional distribution of the data $p_{\texttt{data}}(Y \mid \mathbf{x})$. This follows from the analogous proof for unconditional GANs in Goodfellow et al. (2014), since that proof applies to modeling any arbitrary distribution over $Y$, including $p_{\texttt{data}}(Y \mid \mathbf{x})$ for any $\mathbf{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Conditional GANs enable generation of data conditioned on inputs, ensuring outputs match inputs and appear realistic, improving conditional data modeling. (LLM-inferred)
concepts.recap_md:
- Conditional GANs input $\mathbf{x}$ to both generator and discriminator.
- The discriminator judges if input-output pairs are real or synthetic.
- This ensures generated samples match the conditional data distribution $p_{\texttt{data}}(Y \mid \mathbf{x})$.

concepts.title: Conditional Variational Autoencoders

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: Conditional VAEs model $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x})$ as a marginal over latent variables $\mathbf{z}$ independent of $\mathbf{x}$, encoding information about $\mathbf{y}$ not in $\mathbf{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Conditional VAEs model complex conditional distributions by introducing latent variables encoding information independent of the conditioning input, enabling richer and more accurate predictions. (LLM-inferred)
concepts.recap_md:
- cVAEs model $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x})$ via latent variable marginalization.
- Latent $\mathbf{z}$ encodes information about $\mathbf{y}$ independent of $\mathbf{x}$.
- cVAEs have encoders and decoders conditioned on $\mathbf{x}$ and trained similarly to VAEs.

slots.motivation: Conditional VAEs model complex conditional distributions by introducing latent variables encoding information independent of the conditioning input, enabling richer and more accurate predictions. (LLM-inferred)
slots.key_passage:
- cVAEs model $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x})$ via latent variable marginalization.
- Latent $\mathbf{z}$ encodes information about $\mathbf{y}$ independent of $\mathbf{x}$.
- cVAEs have encoders and decoders conditioned on $\mathbf{x}$ and trained similarly to VAEs.

key_passage.text: In conditional VAEs (cVAEs), we restrict our attention to latent variables \mathbf{z} that are independent of the inputs we are conditioning on, so we have: $$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{z}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x})p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})d\mathbf{z} \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{cVAE likelihood model} \end{aligned}$$

motivation.text: The idea is that \mathbf{z} should only encode bits of information about \mathbf{y} that are *independent* from whatever \mathbf{x} already tells us about \mathbf{y}.

example.text: For example, suppose that we are trying to predict the motion of a billiard ball bouncing around in a video sequence. We are given a single frame \mathbf{x} and asked to predict the next frame \mathbf{y}. Only knowing \mathbf{x} we can't know whether the ball will move up, down, diagonally, and so on, but we *can* know what color the ball will be in the next frame (it must be the same as the previous frame) and the rough position on the screen of the ball (it can't have moved too far). Therefore, the only missing information about \mathbf{y}, given we know \mathbf{x}, is the velocity of the ball. Naturally, then, if the model learns to interpret \mathbf{z} as coding for velocity, we would have a perfect prediction p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x}) (one that places max likelihood on the observed next frame \mathbf{y}), and marginalizing over all the possible \mathbf{z} values would place max likelihood on the data (p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x})). This is what ends up happening in a cVAE (or, to be precise, it is one solution that maximizes the cVAE objective; it is not guaranteed to be the solution that is arrived at, but it is a good model of what tends to happen in practice).

concepts.title: Conditional Autoregressive Models

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: To condition autoregressive models on inputs $\mathbf{x}$, concatenate $\mathbf{x}$ as a prefix to the sequence of $y$ values, yielding a factorized conditional probability model.
concepts.content:
Autoregressive models are already modeling a sequence of conditional distributions. To condition them on some inputs $\mathbf{x}$, we can simply concatenate $\mathbf{x}$ as a prefix to the sequence of $y$ values we are modeling, yielding the new sequence: $[x_1, \ldots, x_m, y_1, \ldots, y_n]$. The probability model factorizes as:
$$\begin{aligned}
    p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n p_{\theta}(y_i \bigm | y_1, \ldots, y_{i-1}, x_1, \ldots, x_m)
\end{aligned}$$
Each distribution in this product is a prediction of the next item in a sequence given the previous items, which is no different than what we had for unconditional autoregressive models. Therefore, the tools for modeling unconditional autoregressive distributions are also appropriate for modeling conditional autoregressive distributions. From an implementation perspective, the same exact code will handle both cases, just depending on whether you prefix the sequence or not.
concepts.motivation_md: Conditional autoregressive models allow us to incorporate additional input information $\mathbf{x}$ into sequence modeling, enabling predictions that depend on context or conditioning variables.
concepts.recap_md:
- Conditional autoregressive models prepend conditioning inputs $\mathbf{x}$ to the sequence of $y$ values.
- The conditional probability factorizes as $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}) = \prod_i p_{\theta}(y_i|y_{<i}, \mathbf{x})$.
- Implementation is the same as unconditional autoregressive models, differing only by prefixing the input sequence.

concepts.title: Conditional Diffusion Models

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: Conditional diffusion models concatenate conditioning variables $\mathbf{x}$ into the input to the denoising function, enabling the model to generate outputs conditioned on $\mathbf{x}$.
concepts.content:
Diffusion models are quite similar to autoregressive models and can be made conditional in a similar way. All we need to do is concatenate the conditioning variables, $\mathbf{x}$, into the input to the denoising function:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \hat{\mathbf{y}}_{t-1} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}_t, t, \mathbf{x})
\end{aligned}$$
Both diffusion models and autoregressive models convert generative modeling into a sequence of supervised prediction problems. To make them conditional is therefore just as easy as conditioning a supervised learner on more observations. If the original training pairs are $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, we can condition on additional paired observations $\mathbf{c}$ by augmenting the pairs to become $\{[\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{c}^{(i)}], \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$.

An example where we condition on text is shown in
@fig-conditional_generative_models-text_conditional_diffusion_model.
The intuition is that if we give $f_{\theta}$ a description of the image as an additional input, then it can do a better job at solving its prediction task. Because of this, $f_{\theta}$ will become sensitive to the text command, and if you give different text it will denoise toward a different image—an image that matches that text! In @sec-VLMs-CLIP we will describe in more detail a particular neural architecture for text-to-image synthesis, which is based on this intuition.

(see figure: Text-conditional diffusion model.)

- They convert generative modeling into supervised prediction conditioned on $\mathbf{x}$.
- Conditioning on text enables generating images matching textual descriptions.

concepts.title: Structured Prediction in Vision
concepts.one_liner: Conditional generative models are suitable for structured prediction problems in vision where outputs are high-dimensional and structured, such as label maps or geometry estimations.
concepts.content:
Whenever you want to make a prediction of an *image*, conditional generative models are a suitable modeling choice. But how often do we really want to predict images? Yes, image colorization is one example, but isn't that more of a graphics problem? Most problems in vision are about predicting labels or geometry, right?

Well yes, but what does label prediction look like? The input is an image and the output is a label map. In image classification the output might just be a single class, but more generally, in object detection and semantic segmentation, we want a label for each part of the image. The target output in these problems is high-dimensional and structured.

Or consider geometry estimation: the output is a depth map, or a voxel grid, or a mesh, and so on. All these are high-dimensional structured objects. concepts.title: Image-to-Image Translation
concepts.one_liner: Image-to-image translation maps an input image to an output image, treating images as arrays and translating between different views or representations of the data.
concepts.content:
Image-to-image problems are mapping problems where the input is an image and the output is also an image, where we will here think of an image as any array of size $N \times M \times C$ (height by width by number of channels). These problems are very common in computer vision. Examples include colorization, next frame prediction, depth map estimation, and semantic segmentation (a per-pixel label map is also an image, just with $K$ channels, one for each label, rather than three channels, one for each color channel).

One way to think about all these problems is as *translating* from one view of the data to another; for example, semantic segmentation is a translation from viewing the world in terms of its colors to viewing the world in terms of its semantics. This perspective yields the problem of **image-to-image translation** @pix2pix2017; just like we can translate from English to French, can we translate from pixels to semantics, or perhaps from a photographic depiction of scene to a painting of that same scene?

concepts.title: Image-to-Image Translation with a Conditional GAN
concepts.one_liner: Image-to-image translation can be performed using a conditional GAN, where a generator maps an input image to an output image and a discriminator evaluates realism.
concepts.content:
One approach to image-to-image translation is to use a conditional GAN, as was popularized in the "pix2pix" paper @pix2pix2017 (whose method we will follow here). To illustrate this approach, we look at the problem of translating a facade layout map into a photo. In this setting, the conditioning information (input) is a layout map showing where all the architectural elements are positioned on the facade (i.e., a semantic segmentation image of the facade, with colors indicating where the windows, doors, and so on are located), and the output is a matching photo.

The generator therefore maps an image to an image so we will implement it with an image-to-image neural architecture. This could be a convolutional neural network (CNN), or a transformer; following the pix2pix paper we will use a U-Net (a CNN with accordion-shaped skip connections; see @sec-convolutional_neural_nets-unet). The discriminator maps the output image to a real-versus-synthetic score (a scalar), so for the discriminator we will use a regular CNN (just like the ones used for image classification). Here is the full architecture (@fig-conditional_generative_models-pix2pix_facades_arch):

(see figure: The pix2pix @pix2pix2017 model applied to translating a facade layout map into a photo of the facade. The model was trained on the CMP Facades Database @Tylecek13 and the input and ground truth...)

Notice that we have omitted the noise inputs here; instead the generator only takes as input the image $\mathbf{x}$. It turns out that in this setting the noise is not really a necessary input, and many implementations omit it. This is because the input image $\mathbf{x}$ has enough entropy by itself, and you don't necessarily need additional noise to create variety in the outputs of the model. The downside of

concepts.title: PatchGAN
concepts.one_liner: A PatchGAN discriminator scores each patch in an output image as real or fake and averages these scores as the total loss.
concepts.content:
An architecture for image-to-image tasks is a **PatchGAN** discriminator @pix2pix2017, in which we score each *patch* in the output image as real or fake and take the average over patch scores as our total loss:
$$\begin{aligned}    d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{i=0}^N \sum_{j=0}^M d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}(\mathbf{x}[i:i+k,j:j+k], \mathbf{y}[i:i+k,j:j+k])
\end{aligned}$$
where $k \times k$ is the patch size. Notice that this operation is equivalent to the sliding window action of CNN, so $d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}$ can simply be implemented as a CNN that outputs a $2 \times N \times M$ feature map of real-versus-synthetic scores. Naturally, patches can be sampled at different strides and resolutions, depending on the exact architecture of the CNN $d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: PatchGAN discriminators focus on local image patches to better capture high-frequency details and texture realism in image-to-image translation tasks.

- PatchGAN discriminator scores each $k \times k$ patch in the output image as real or fake.
- The total loss is the average over all patch scores.
- Implemented as a CNN producing a feature map of real-versus-synthetic scores.

concepts.title: Unpaired Image-to-Image Translation
concepts.one_liner: Unpaired image-to-image translation learns mappings between image domains without paired training data, enabling style transfer and other tasks where paired data is unavailable.
concepts.content:
In the preceding section we saw how to solve image-to-image translation by treating it just like a supervised regression problem, except using a learned loss function given by a GAN discriminator. This approach works great when we have lots of training data pairs $\{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\}$ to learn from. Unfortunately, very often, paired training data is hard to obtain. For example, consider the task of translating a photo into a Cezanne painting (@fig-conditional_generative_models-cyclegan_teaser):

(see figure: A style transfer example from the CycleGAN paper @CycleGAN2017 *Input photo source*: Alexei A. Efros.)

The task depicted here is to predict: What would it have looked like if Cezanne had stood at this riverbank and painted it?

How could this be done? We can't have solved it with paired training data because, in this setting, paired data is extremely hard to come by. We would have to resurrect Cezanne and ask him to paint for us a bunch of new scenes, one for each photo in our desired training set. But is all that effort really necessary? You and I, as humans, can certainly imagine the answer to the previous question. We know what Cezanne's style looks like and can reason about the changes that would have to occur to make the photo match his style. Dabs of paint would have to replace the photographic pixels, and the colors should take on more pastel tones. We can imagine the necessary stylistic changes because we have seen many Cezanne paintings before, even though we didn't see them paired with a photograph of the exact same scenes. Let's now see how we can give a machine this same ability. We call this setting the **unpaired translation** setting, and distinguish it from **paired translation** as indicated in @fig-conditional_generative_models-paired_vs_unpaired.

concepts.recap_md:
- Paired image-to-image translation requires matched input-output pairs.
- Unpaired translation learns mappings without paired data.
- This enables style transfer where paired examples are rare or impossible.

concepts.title: CycleGAN
concepts.one_liner: CycleGAN introduces cycle-consistency, ensuring that translating from $X$ to $Y$ and back returns to the original input.
concepts.content:
Cycle-consistency, introduced by CycleGAN @CycleGAN2017, DualGAN @yi2017dualgan, and DiscoGAN @kim2017learning (all essentially the same model), means that if we translate from domain $X$ to $Y$ and then back from $Y$ to $X$, we should arrive where we started. For example, translating "apple" from English to French yields "pomme," and translating "pomme" back to English returns "apple." In natural language processing, this idea is known as backtranslation.

We can check the quality of a translation system for an unfamiliar language using this trick: if translating back does not return the original word, the translation model likely failed. This is because language translation is roughly one-to-one: each English word usually has an equivalent French word. Cycle-consistency losses act as regularizers encouraging the learned mapping to be roughly one-to-one. The cycle-consistency losses from CycleGAN are:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{cyc}}(\mathbf{x};g_{\theta},f_{\psi}) &= \left\lVert\mathbf{x} - f_{\psi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))\right\rVert_1\\
    \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{cyc}}(\mathbf{y};g_{\theta},f_{\psi}) &= \left\lVert\mathbf{y} - g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y}))\right\rVert_1
\end{aligned}
$$

Adding this loss to @eq-conditional_generative_models-x_to_y_GAN_learning_problem yields the complete CycleGAN objective:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    \arg\min_{\theta,\psi}\max_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}^{Y}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}^{Y}(\mathbf{y})) + \left\lVert\mathbf{x} - f_{\psi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))\right\rVert_1 + \\
    \log d_{\phi}^{X}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}^{X}(\mathbf{x})) + \left\lVert\mathbf{y} - g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y}))\right\rVert_1 \big]
\end{aligned}
$$

This model translates from domain $X$ to domain $Y$ and back, such that the outputs in domain $Y$ look realistic according to a domain $Y$ discriminator, and vice versa for domain $X$, and the mappings are cycle-consistent: one complete cycle from $X$ to $Y$ and back should arrive where it started (and vice versa). A diagram for this whole process is given in

(see figure: CycleGAN schematic. Figure derived from @CycleGAN2017)
concepts.motivation_md: Cycle-consistency ensures that translations between domains are reversible, helping to learn mappings that are roughly one-to-one and improving the quality of unsupervised domain translation models like CycleGAN.
concepts.recap_md:
- Cycle-consistency means translating from $X$ to $Y$ and back returns the original input.
- CycleGAN uses cycle-consistency losses as regularizers to enforce one-to-one mappings.
- The full CycleGAN objective combines adversarial losses with cycle-consistency losses for both domains.

Adding the cycle-consistency loss to the conditional generative model learning problem @eq-conditional_generative_models-x_to_y_GAN_learning_problem yields the complete CycleGAN objective:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    \arg\min_{\theta,\psi}\max_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}^{Y}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}^{Y}(\mathbf{y})) + \left\lVert\mathbf{x} - f_{\psi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))\right\rVert_1 + \\
    \log d_{\phi}^{X}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}^{X}(\mathbf{x})) + \left\lVert\mathbf{y} - g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y}))\right\rVert_1 \big]
\end{aligned}
$$
concepts.motivation_md: This objective integrates adversarial and cycle-consistency losses to train models that translate between domains while ensuring reversibility and realistic outputs.
concepts.recap_md:
- CycleGAN objective combines adversarial losses with cycle-consistency losses.
- It optimizes mappings $g_{\theta}$ and $f_{\psi}$ with discriminators $d_{\phi}^X$ and $d_{\phi}^Y$.
- The losses enforce realistic translation and cycle-consistency.

concepts.title: general-purpose conditional generative models
concepts.one_liner: Conditional generative models provide a unified and simple solution to diverse structured prediction problems in vision.
concepts.content: Many problems in vision can be phrased as structured prediction, and conditional generative models are a great approach to these problems. They provide a unified and simple solution to a diverse array of problems. A current trend in computer vision (and all of artificial intelligence) is to replace bespoke systems for specific kinds of structured prediction—object detectors, image captioning systems, and so on—with general-purpose conditional generative models. This is one reason why this book does not focus much on special-purpose systems that solve specific problems in vision—because the trend is toward general-purpose modeling tools.
concepts.motivation_md: General-purpose conditional generative models simplify and unify solutions to many vision tasks, replacing specialized systems with flexible, broadly applicable models.
concepts.recap_md:
- Many vision problems are structured prediction tasks.
- Conditional generative models offer a unified approach.
- The trend is toward general-purpose models instead of bespoke systems.

prereq.rationale: Structured prediction in vision uses conditional generative models as a suitable modeling choice for predicting high-dimensional structured outputs like label maps or geometry, as stated in the passage.

Understanding the failure of point prediction in multimodal distributions requires knowledge of conditional generative models, which provide a framework for modeling the distribution of outputs conditioned on inputs, rather than a single point prediction.
Understanding general-purpose conditional generative models requires knowledge of conditional generative models, as the former are a broad application of the latter to diverse vision problems.
General-purpose conditional generative models are used to solve structured prediction problems in vision, so understanding structured prediction is a prerequisite.
Image-to-Image Translation with a Conditional GAN is a technique that directly applies to the problem defined by Image-to-Image Translation, thus requires understanding the problem definition first.
PatchGAN discriminator is a specific architecture used in image-to-image translation with conditional GANs, so understanding the conditional GAN technique requires knowing PatchGAN.

Unpaired Image-to-Image Translation is an extension of the image-to-image translation problem to the unpaired data setting, so it requires understanding the original image-to-image translation problem.
Unpaired learning is the learning paradigm underlying unpaired image-to-image translation, so understanding unpaired image-to-image translation requires understanding unpaired learning.
CycleGAN is a method for unpaired image-to-image translation, so it requires understanding the unpaired image-to-image translation problem.
The CycleGAN objective is the specific loss function used to train CycleGAN models, so understanding the objective requires understanding the CycleGAN model.
The CycleGAN objective explicitly includes the cycle-consistency loss term, so understanding the objective requires understanding cycle-consistency.

overlay.rationale: Structured prediction methods model joint structure in the output space and include conditional generative modeling as a specific approach that models full distributions over joint outputs, making conditional generative models a special case within structured prediction.
General-purpose conditional generative models are a current trend in vision for structured prediction problems, so they are topically related to the idea of structured prediction in vision.
Backtranslation is the natural language processing term for cycle-consistency, so these concepts are closely related and cross-referencing is helpful.
